summary: Arabic greetings are fixed formulas with fixed answers: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ → وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ, صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ → صَبَاحُ النُّورِ, مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ → مَسَاءُ النُّورِ, شُكْرًا → عَفْوًا. There is no polite “you” like Sie or 您, but every formula that contains “you” changes with the listener: كَيْفَ حَالُكَ to a man, كَيْفَ حَالُكِ to a woman, كَيْفَ حَالُكُمْ to several people — and an apology follows the speaker: a man says آسِفٌ, a woman آسِفَةٌ. The Standard formulas are understood everywhere; everyday speech adds regional ones (كِيفَك، إِزَّيَّك، شْلَوْنَك).

blocks.caption: “I am sorry” follows the speaker instead: آسِفٌ (a man), آسِفَةٌ (a woman), آسِفُونَ (men or mixed), آسِفَاتٌ (women); عُذْرًا never changes.

blocks.title: Register.
blocks.text: Fine everywhere, also formal: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ، صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ، إِلَى اللِّقَاءِ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ، تَشَرَّفْنَا. Everyday and friendly: أَهْلًا، مَرْحَبًا، مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ، أَرَاكَ لَاحِقًا. Respect comes from titles, not from the pronoun: يَا أُسْتَاذُ (sir, teacher), يَا سَيِّدَتِي (madam), حَضْرَتُكَ.

blocks.title: Answer with the answer.
blocks.text: صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّورِ, not repeated; and أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا (welcome, to a guest) is not عَفْوًا (you’re welcome, after thanks).
Many formulas are frozen accusatives with tanwīn: شُكْرًا، عَفْوًا، مَرْحَبًا، أَهْلًا، عُذْرًا — pronounce the final -n: šukran, ʿafwan.

askYourself: Am I meeting someone, leaving, or is someone going to bed?
Is there a fixed answer? (السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ → وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ; صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ → صَبَاحُ النُّورِ)
Does the formula contain “you”? → -ka to a man, -ki to a woman, -kum to several people.
Is it about me (آسِفٌ / آسِفَةٌ)? → it follows my own gender.

traps: كَيْفَ حَالُكَ to a woman sounds wrong: it is حَالُكِ (-ki).
صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is only an answer; you do not start with it.
مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ greets; it is not “good night” before sleep (تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ).
آسِفٌ / آسِفَةٌ agrees with the speaker, not with the listener.
عَلَيْكُمْ in السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ stays plural even to one person.

quiz.why: عَفْوًا = you’re welcome; أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا welcomes a guest.

quiz.q: Good night, to a man going to bed:
quiz.why: مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ greets in the evening; تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ is said at bedtime.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew שָׁלוֹם is the same word as سَلَام (שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם = السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ), and Hebrew also changes formulas with the listener: מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ / מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ like كَيْفَ حَالُكَ / حَالُكِ.
German chooses by formality — Wie geht’s dir? / Wie geht es Ihnen? — where Arabic chooses by the listener’s gender.
Chinese shows politeness with 您 (你好 / 您好) and has no gender in “you” at all.
